content: Eating disorders are challenging to treat, requiring significant time, effort, and financial resources. Certain factors, such as being young, female, and engaging in dieting behaviors, have been consistently associated with an increased risk of developing eating disorders. However, there is currently limited evidence to suggest that any specific type of prevention program is effective in reducing the risk of eating disorders. Additionally, there is concern that some interventions may inadvertently cause harm. The primary objectives of this review were to evaluate whether eating disorder prevention programs for children and adolescents are effective in achieving the following outcomes: (1) fostering healthy eating attitudes and behaviors; (2) enhancing protective psychological factors; (3) promoting satisfactory physical health; (4) producing long-term, sustainable, and positive effects on mental and physical health; and (5) ensuring that the programs do not result in harmful consequences for mental or physical health. To identify relevant studies, researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Controlled Trial Register (CCTR), as well as other biomedical and social science databases. They also reviewed reference lists of identified articles and consulted with experts in the field. The inclusion criteria for this review required randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that focused on eating disorder prevention programs for children and adolescents without a known DSM-IV diagnosis of an eating disorder. Eligible trials needed to include a control group and at least one objective outcome measure, such as body mass index (BMI), or a standardized psychological measure applied to both the intervention and control groups before and after the intervention. From the search, 1,016 titles were initially identified. After critical appraisal by two independent reviewers, 22 studies using randomized controlled trial methodologies were selected for further evaluation. Of these, 12 studies met the inclusion criteria. The analysis of two prevention programs that utilized a media literacy and advocacy approach demonstrated a reduction in the internalization or acceptance of societal appearance ideals at a follow-up period of 3 to 6 months. The standardized mean difference (SMD) for this effect was -0.28, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from -0.51 to -0.05. However, there was insufficient evidence to support the effectiveness of five programs aimed at addressing eating attitudes, behaviors, and other adolescent issues in either the general population or high-risk groups. Similarly, there was insufficient evidence to support the effectiveness of two programs designed to improve self-esteem. Data from two didactic eating disorder awareness programs could not be combined for analysis. Importantly, there was no evidence to suggest that any of the prevention programs included in the review caused harm to participants. However, the findings of this review do not allow for definitive conclusions regarding the overall impact of eating disorder prevention programs for children and adolescents. While one significant pooled effect was observed, it is not sufficient to draw firm conclusions. Additionally, the meta-analysis is currently being revised to account for the influence of cluster-randomized trials.
